tool.title: India
tool.excerpt: The Vijayanagara Empire built a powerful military-fiscal state that fostered a flourishing, distinctively South Indian Hindu culture. During this era, Sikhism emerged in the Punjab, promoting an egalitarian devotion that transcended traditional Hindu and Muslim boundaries. The Mughal Empire ushered in two centuries of economic expansion and relative peace, leaving a lasting legacy of administrative centralisation and cultural synthesis. PHOTO: AFP Published Nov 10, 2026, 11:02 AM Updated Nov 10, 2026, 11:34 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum returned the remains of 39 Naga people to their community in Nagaland.
The Oxford museum has more than 6,000 objects representing Naga culture – the largest collection in the world – and is giving back “ancestral human remains”, mainly skulls, to the Naga people.

“I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person.” The Naga people once practised headhunting, severing the heads of enemies as trophies, but also kept the heads of their own chiefs “at the centre of the villages”, and one of the remains is a chief’s head, said anthropologist Dolly Kikon, a member of Nagaland’s Lotha-Naga community.
The handover follows wider museum moves to review colonial-era collections and return human remains.
The museum has already returned remains to Indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.

Almost 30 people from the community based in north-eastern Nagaland, a mountainous state bordering Myanmar, travelled to Britain for the ceremony, which the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven, called a “historic moment”.

The handover at the Pitt Rivers Museum came as part of a broader trend among Western museums reassessing how they acquired exhibits from other cultures, particularly human remains, and in some cases returning them.
The Pitt Rivers, an ethnographic museum founded in the 19th century, has already handed back human remains to Indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the US.
The Naga remains were brought to Oxford between 1910 and 1940.
Naga leaders will bury the remains together under a joint memorial.
The remains were already “on their way to Heathrow” airport, the museum director said, after overcoming “so much red tape everywhere”.
The museum removed all human remains from display only in 2020, much later than most museums, and still has around 2,700 remains in storage, she told AFP.
Naga tribal leaders united for the handover and planned to bury the remains together under a joint memorial in a park.
The museum says on its website that items collected during this era were “frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given”.
“The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate,” Vihienuo said.
During a speech, as both sides signed a formal agreement on the handover, Van Broekhoven hailed it as “a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations”.
‘Respectful rest’ Housed in a Victorian Gothic building, the museum is a dark, atmospheric space with glass cases crammed with objects, many with handwritten labels.
“It’s been six years of working alongside each other on a very delicate matter,” the museum director said.
Most were collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.
While in Oxford, the delegation met descendants of one of the anthropologists.

sentences: (File Photo: ITG) By: India Today World Desk London , Nov 10, 2026 23:54 IST Last Updated Nov 10, 2026 23:54 IST Published by India Today Web Desk Nov 10, 2026 23:54 IST The Pitt Rivers Museum at the University of Oxford has handed over the remains of 39 Naga ancestors for their return to India, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
It includes the remains of Naga people taken during the colonial era and held at the museum for decades.

Advertisement Since 2020, the museum has worked with the FNR and RRaD teams, tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities across the Naga homeland to decide how the ancestors should be cared for and returned.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation approached the museum earlier this year to seek the return of the ancestral remains.

Since 2020, the museum has worked with the FNR and RRaD teams, tribal Hohos, elders, churches and communities across the Naga homeland to decide how the ancestors should be cared for and returned, according to PTI.
"In February 2026, the University of Oxford received a claim from the FNR for 40 ancestral remains kept in the Pitt Rivers Museum.
The claim followed the university's procedures for the return of cultural objects and was agreed by the Oxford University Council on July 13, 2026," the museum said.

After the ceremony, the ancestors will finally return home, accompanied by a Naga delegation, including leaders and elders of several Naga tribe Hohos, together with members of the FNR and RRaD," the museum said.
A 30-member delegation from Nagaland received the remains at a ceremony in Oxford on Monday.

advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story "I feel honoured that we walked alongside our partners to find the path to return for these 39 Naga ancestors, who have been away from their homeland for far too long," said Professor Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum.
The museum holds the world's largest collection of Naga material, much of it gathered by colonial administrators in the early 20th century.
The council approved the return of 39 ancestral remains but declined to return one other remain because it did not have a "clear provenance as Naga".
Most of the Naga remains in the collection were brought to Oxford by Hutton and another administrator-anthropologist, James Philip Mills, between 1910 and 1940.
The return was supported by the Homebound Project, which funds the repatriation of ancestral remains and cultural belongings from UK institutions to Indigenous communities.
The 39 Naga ancestors will now be taken to India and laid to rest beneath a joint memorial in Nagaland.
Most of the remains are skulls and will be given a "respectful rest", according to Naga tribal leaders, who plan to bury them beneath a joint memorial in a park in Nagaland.
The remains were displayed at the museum until 2020, when it removed all human remains from public display.
Especially inspiring is the beautiful way that collective work and shared action kept engagement growing to become a Naga-wide movement of healing and unification," Van Broekhoven said.
"Following this decision, the Pitt Rivers Museum has been working closely with the Nagas to agree on a date for the handover ceremony.

tool.excerpt: On 9 November 2026, an explosion and fire at the HABAŞ Demir Çelik iron and steel plant in Aliağa, in Turkey's İzmir Province, killed 18 workers and injured at least 12 others. A crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed into an electric arc furnace during the casting of molten steel, setting off a blast and a fire that destroyed part of the casting platform and damaged a natural gas line. HABAŞ described the accident as occurring during scheduled maintenance on one of its arc furnaces. Search and rescue work continued that evening for workers trapped beneath the wreckage. == Background == HABAŞ Demir Çelik is the steelmaking arm of HABAŞ (Habaş Sınai ve Tıbbi Gazlar İstihsal Endüstrisi A.Ş.), a privately owned Turkish group whose Aliağa operations also include port facilities. It is one of the country's largest steel producers. The plant is located on the Yeni Foça road about 60 kilometres (37 mi) north of İzmir and has operated since 1987. Aliağa is a heavy-industrial district and one of Turkey's main ship breaking centres. The plant has a long record of fatal and serious accidents. Evrensel said that no fewer than 11 workers had died at the plant in the last decade. The previous deadliest incident was in 1999, when a falling ladle killed four workers. Two deaths came in the weeks before the November 2026 blast. Hakan Doğan, 55, died on 21 October 2026 after falling about 8 metres (26 ft) from a ladder while working for a subcontractor, and Eyüp Eğinli was killed on 5 November 2026 when a heavy vehicle tyre exploded while being inflated. The disaster fed a wider argument about workplace safety in Turkey. The independent Health and Safety Labour Watch (İSİG) counted more than 200 worker deaths in each of the five months to September 2026, the first such run since it began publishing figures in 2013. == Explosion == At the time of the explosion, around 200 workers were present at the factory, with 100 more having stayed home because of a boiler replacement operation. Evrensel said that no fewer than 11 workers had died at the plant in the last decade. The previous deadliest incident was in 1999, when a falling ladle killed four workers. Two deaths came in the weeks before the November 2026 blast. Hakan Doğan, 55, died on 21 October 2026 after falling about 8 metres (26 ft) from a ladder while working for a subcontractor, and Eyüp Eğinli was killed on 5 November 2026 when a heavy vehicle tyre exploded while being inflated. A crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed into an electric arc furnace during the casting of molten steel, setting off a blast and a fire that destroyed part of the casting platform and damaged a natural gas line. HABAŞ described the accident as occurring during scheduled maintenance on one of its arc furnaces. Search and rescue work continued that evening for workers trapped beneath the wreckage. == Background == HABAŞ Demir Çelik is the steelmaking arm of HABAŞ (Habaş Sınai ve Tıbbi Gazlar İstihsal Endüstrisi A.Ş.), a privately owned Turkish group whose Aliağa operations also include port facilities. It is one of the country's largest steel producers. The plant is located on the Yeni Foça road about 60 kilometres (37 mi) north of İzmir and has operated since 1987. Aliağa is a heavy-industrial district and one of Turkey's main ship breaking centres. The plant has a long record of fatal and serious accidents. Evrensel said that no fewer than 11 workers had died at the plant in the last decade. The previous deadliest incident was in 1999, when a falling ladle killed four workers. Two deaths came in the weeks before the November 2026 blast. Hakan Doğan, 55, died on 21 October 2026 after falling about 8 metres (26 ft) from a ladder while working for a subcontractor, and Eyüp Eğinli was killed on 5 November 2026 when a heavy vehicle tyre exploded while being inflated. The disaster fed a wider argument about workplace safety in Turkey. The independent Health and Safety Labour Watch (İSİG) counted more than 200 worker deaths in each of the five months to September 2026, the first such run since it began publishing figures in 2013. == Explosion == At the time of the explosion, around 200 workers were present at the factory, with 100 more having stayed home because of a boiler replacement operation. HABAŞ described the accident as occurring during scheduled maintenance on one of its arc furnaces. Search and rescue work continued that evening for workers trapped beneath the wreckage. == Background == HABAŞ Demir Çelik is the steelmaking arm of HABAŞ (Habaş Sınai ve Tıbbi Gazlar İstihsal Endüstrisi A.Ş.), a privately owned Turkish group whose Aliağa operations also include port facilities. It is one of the country's largest steel producers. The plant is located on the Yeni Foça road about 60 kilometres (37 mi) north of İzmir and has operated since 1987. Aliağa is a heavy-industrial district and one of Turkey's main ship breaking centres. The plant has a long record of fatal and serious accidents. Evrensel said that no fewer than 11 workers had died at the plant in the last decade. The previous deadliest incident was in 1999, when a falling ladle killed four workers. Two deaths came in the weeks before the November 2026 blast. Hakan Doğan, 55, died on 21 October 2026 after falling about 8 metres (26 ft) from a ladder while working for a subcontractor, and Eyüp Eğinli was killed on 5 November 2026 when a heavy vehicle tyre exploded while being inflated. The disaster fed a wider argument about workplace safety in Turkey. The source spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter. It was not clear if Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé would meet directly with Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele. The visit comes as Bukele has ramped up his offensive against Haiti’s gangs with at least 2,500 Salvadoran forces now operating in Haiti. The offensive began in October after four Salvadoran aviation technicians went missing in an attack by gangs. Since, Bukele has sought to project an image as a crusader on crime coming to vanquish Haitian gangs, which control whole parts of Haiti’s territory and are deeply entwined with some of the country’s political elite. On Sunday, Haitian police and Salvadoran soldiers destroyed a home of Wilson Joseph, the leader of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti’s most powerful gangs. The operation was first reported by Haitian media and confirmed by Damian Merlo, a lobbyist working for El Salvador’s government. The offensive did not kill the leader, better known as Lanmò San Jou, and Haitian gang leaders regularly cycle between a number of houses. Last Friday, two days before the operation, Bukele posted on the social media platform X asking for the location of Joseph’s house in Haitian Creole. “Give us the exact address, and we’ll destroy it,” he wrote.
